Hi [~accountid:5f32a6e98d89e300461b43ed] Thank you for raising the ticket!

I will analyze this in two parts: reclassification risks and legal/operational risks.

# *Reclassification Risks*

Even if the AR is officially enforced by fleet owners, it still poses a risk for us, as it can be easily traced back to us. If a regulatory body investigates, it could be interpreted as us imposing our instructions on couriers, with fleet owners merely acting as intermediaries. In other words, we could be seen as +exercising indirect control over the couriers+.

# *Legal and Operational Risks*

You mentioned that the agreement would not be documented in writing, which raises some concerns.

* +Enforceability Issues+: Without a written agreement, proving that such an arrangement exists could be difficult, particularly if we need to terminate a contract due to couriers not meeting performance expectations.
* +Legal Compliance+: To my knowledge, Czech law requires transparency in performance expectations and termination conditions. A verbal agreement may not be sufficient in case of disputes.

*Recommendations for mitigating the risks*

* Set the 30% AR as an average for the entire fleet, rather than an individual courier requirement. (If this was already the intention, I’m emphasizing it separately for clarity.)
* Ensure fleets have the freedom to decide how they manage their couriers' performance.
* Specify this expectation in a written agreement or addendum.

*Conclusion*

This approach carries risks, but following these recommendations should help mitigate direct exposure. Additionally, try to avoid language that suggests imposed requirements. Instead, frame them as expectations or something similar.

Let me know if you have any further questions!

I hope your day is going well.

 

We received the attached SLA from legal with changes that they have accepted and also the following reasons provided for not being able to accept other suggested changes. The reasons provided are as follows:

 

 

# Firstly, it is our view that Alexforbes Health is the operator and not the responsible party nor are we the “controller” in the DSA addendum. The controller exercises control of the personal information whereas the processor processes personal information on behalf of the controller. In this instance, Alexforbes Health is the processer of personal information while the client is the controller.

 

# Importantly, and for purposes of the Protection of Personal Information Act, 2013, the client appoints Alexforbes Health to provide health care consulting services to its employees, we act solely on the client’s instructions relating to the data subject. Consequently, we are restricted and wholly dependent on the instructions from the client as set out in full in terms of the SLA. In terms of the relationship:

 

2.1       the client gives Alexforbes Health specific and comprehensive instructions on how to give health care consulting services to their employees, by for example restricting the medical schemes that they are allowed to advise them on;

 

2.2       Alexforbes Health’s discretion is constrained by the client’s instructions. We cannot decide to advise the employees on medical schemes that the employer has not authorised them to provide advice on within the bounds of the activity. Alexforbes Health’s decision making is wholly dependent on the instructions from the employer;

 

2.3       the client has the knowledge and expertise to properly understand and carry out the activity themselves, but they have decided to outsource it to Alexforbes Health in terms of the SLA.

 

2.4       To this end, and by way of example, we refer you to clause 7.5.1 of the SLA which provides _In the performance of its obligations, Alexforbes shall: provide the Services promptly, in a professional manner and in accordance with the Law, the_ *_written directives of the Client_* as well as 7.5.3 which provides that Alexforbes *_shall adhere to all reasonable procedures requested by the Client;_*

 

2.5       Therefore we re-iterate that the SLA requires the client to determine why the personal information is processed, because the SLA requires Alexforbes Health to render the services in accordance with the client’s written directives and adhere to all their reasonable requested procedures.

 

# Considering the above, Alexforbes Health cannot accept the client’s DSA addendum. Ultimately, as the operator, we process personal information of health consulting members (the data subjects) on behalf of employers as the responsible parties.

 

# Lastly, we have resolved that the original personal information clause in our SLA should remain in place as they appropriately outline the role of Alexforbes Health as the operator of personal information and the client as the responsible party. This is a standard we have adopted across the board with all our clients.

 

 

I hope this clarifies why we cannot accept the DSA addendum.

Dear Damir,

Thank you for your data subject rights request, which we received on 21 January 2025.

We take your privacy seriously. As a part of this commitment, we would like to clarify Bolt’s practices in relation to collecting and processing your location information.

Bolt may use your geolocation data for various purposes, including to suggest new rides and destinations depending on the consents you have provided in your Bolt app. You can always disable these specific notifications, without disabling all Bolt notifications. Further information in this regard can be found in our privacy notice available at [https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides] .

Additionally, please note the following:

* Bolt starts collecting your location data when you grant permission to tracking it for either ‘All time', ‘While using the App’ or ‘Once’. Bolt asks for such permission on sign-in; however, such permission can be revoked or granted at any time via your device settings (either when a prompt to authorise background use is displayed in the Bolt app or on your own). Your location information is collected only in the foreground. This means that Bolt starts collecting your location data when you open the Bolt app and stops collecting it when you close the Bolt app.
* The permission to share your location data ‘All the time’ applies only to the geofencing feature, which is used to notify you if Bolt is operating in a specific geographic area. Bolt does not, however, store any of your location data in relation to this. iOS and Android devices enable apps to automatically trigger notifications when the user enters a specific geographic area. This does not require the Bolt app to run in the background or mobile data to be used. Apple and Android store this information at their end and automatically trigger those notifications when a user enters a defined geographic area, without sharing the user’s location with Bolt.

*Your rights* 

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

Hi Monika,

As discussed:

*BrightHire - Notice to Interviewees, Redaction*

# The notices/call-recording disclaimers provided to interviewees, and the ability for interviewees to opt-out of being recorded/transcribed are good.
# The disclaimer we include in GoodTime is good. We should require that all interviews be scheduled through GoodTime to ensure that these disclaimers are seen by interviewees in their calendars.

*Opt-Out for Interviewers?*

* We discussed the ability to provide interviewers with an ability to opt-out.
* I mentioned that provided that we make it a formal interview policy requirement to use BrightHire recording and transcriptions, it should be OK for it to be mandatory. However, I indicated that:
** We need to explain the rationale for this to Interviewers in the Interview Policy.
** There needs to be a policy exception where the interviewee has opted-out.
** We need to explain how interviewer data is used in BrightHire and for how long it is kept.

*Retention in BrightHire*

* We need to revisit retention periods in BrightHire.
* We should differentiate between Interviewee and Interviewer retention periods, if possible. If possible, we should try and differentiate between video and text data (i.e. we keep transcription/summaries for longer than video recordings).
* We should keep the retention periods to a *_minimum_*, and I will require Recruitment input to justify why we need to keep this data and for how long.
* I explained that a risk in retaining this data is that those candidate's who are rejected can request a copy of their recruitment data and we would need to provide a copy of BrightHire data, if we retain it.
* We will need to update the Recruitment Privacy Notice once we have agreed on these retention periods.

*Interview Policy*

* We need to prohibit the use of 3rd party transcription tools by Bolt interviewers during external interviews. This is especially important where an interviewee has opted out of BrightHire.
* I suggest that this Policy is stored on Confluence and communicated to Interviewers when they have a scheduled interview (i.e. as part of an interview guidance pack/etc).
* Privacy will input into this Policy but our request is that it is led by the People Recruitment Team.

Thank you.

Dear Volodymyr,

We write further to your recent data subject rights request, which we received on 3 November 2024. Thank you for your patience. We include our response below.

*(1) Information on data sharing with Meta*

Bolt engages with third-party analytics providers such as Appsflyer, which can result in sharing certain user information between Bolt and Meta for marketing and analytics purposes. The extent of such sharing depends on the tracking permissions that a user has enabled in the Bolt app. When an iOS user installs or opens the Bolt app for the first time after downloading it from the App Store, the user is asked whether they wish to opt-in to the App Tracking Transparency (“ATT”) framework in the form of a prompt (“Allow Bolt: Request a Ride to track your activity across other companies' apps and websites?”).

* If the user selects “Allow”, this grants permission for Bolt to track the user’s activity across certain apps and websites. As a result, Bolt may share certain user information such as the user’s identifier for advertisers (“IDFA”), device information and hashed contact information with Meta.
* If the user selects “Ask App Not to Track”, then Bolt will not share user-specific data with Meta in this context. However, Bolt may share certain aggregated information (for example, aggregated performance and postbacks data). Please also note that Meta can retrieve certain user data from Bolt based on other trackers such as web pixels. However, this would not involve the sharing of any user-specific events or postbacks data.

You can find further information on how Bolt processes your personal data in our privacy notice available at[ https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]  . Please note in particular the following section:

* "*_Promotional, marketing and strategic partners_*_: We may share limited data - e.g. your email address - with promotional, marketing and strategic partners so that they can inform you about promotional events and provide you with information and marketing messages about products or services that may be of interest to you._ _In addition, we may share your personal data with marketing platform providers, including advertisers active on social media, advertising networks and third-party data providers._ _The idea is to reach Passengers, to get to know them better, to measure the effectiveness of our advertising on other platforms and on social media sites such as Facebook and Google_."

*(2) Opting-out*

iOS users can change their tracking permissions at any time by taking the following steps in the Bolt app:

# Go to Settings > Privacy & security > Tracking.
# Toggle ‘off’ tracking for any apps where you do not want those apps to track your activity across other apps and websites.

Bolt’s permissions regarding activity tracking can also be removed by logging into a Facebook account and going to Settings & privacy > Your activity and permissions > Apps and websites.

*(3) Your rights*

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

The excerpt from the T&Cs could be interpreted as allowing a suspension *if the billing information is essential for compliance with the law* and falls under the scope of "necessary personal data."

However, we could interpret the clause as giving us justification to suspend, in particular because:

* Clause 11 states that *certain personal data is required for the functioning of the Bolt App and information society service*.
* It also mentions that *removal of personal data may render the use of the Bolt App impossible*.
* If updating billing information is considered essential for legal compliance or service provision, *we could argue that failure to update such data makes service continuation impossible*, justifying a suspension.



For clarity, I am unable to advise on the question whether out T&Cs give this possibility to block the drivers or not, as it is a matter of contractual law/reclass, and not privacy law. I must point out that the clause 11 does not explicitly state that non-compliance with updating information (such as billing details) results in a suspension. Also, as it does not define *billing information as part of the necessary personal data* required to continue using the service, there’s an open-end on whether billing data is really necessary under the clause.

{quote}# *Is there anywhere I can find a list of documents / datapoints that will be subject to this automation process (i.e., the docs that will be automatically reviewed), just for my own awareness?*{quote}

Eventually we want to automate all the renewals in the UK, but this is going to be done gradually, one document type at a time. The specific order in which we launch them depends on the automation performance in the DRY-RUN mode. Once we see that automation can handle a significant share of the document volume with extremely low false positive rate we are going LIVE.

The most likely candidates for the initial launches are:

* UK Driving License
* MOT Test Certificate
* Vehicle Logbook

Eventually we want to rollout automation for the Insurance documents and the Bank statements across the country, as well as city-specific documents like Private Hire Drivers Licence, Private Hire Vehicle License and PCO Badges.

{quote}# *Will the automated processes involve any facial recognition / biometric verification (e.g., of pictures of a user / a photo in their ID)?*{quote}

Eventually yes, but we are not going to do this when launching the first batch of the documents

{quote}# *Will we be creating / leveraging this automated review / acceptance process internally, or using an external third party to do so?*{quote}

The process is internal, except for the text extraction jobs.

For the automation process starts with extracting the text data from the submitted driver’s document, i.e. driver names, address, document issue and expiry date. This job is automated, meaning that we have OCR models doing this. However, in case of a text extraction failure, we fallback to the human reviewers, who handle the missing fields. This workforce is external.

This part of the automation process is handled by Bolt’s own document verification service named Veritas. As far as I understand they have proper legal clearance to do so, but just in case I tag [~accountid:712020:666b819e-7279-4447-91d0-83971e72f35a] who is a GPM for the Identity Platform.

(?) _we wanted to tell them that if they connect to the CCTV, they can’t turn it on for trip A and then turn off for trip B, and so on. 💡 Thanks for sharing this piece of information - this part is extremely important, and *changes our assessment.* *Why?*

* By giving such instructions to the driver, under privacy laws, it will be considered that the drivers are instructed to collect CCTV recordings data and therefore, *Bolt will become responsible for all privacy aspects related to CCTVs* used by these drivers, including: data retention requirements, providing information for passengers as well as drivers, management of user requests (including requests to provide copies of CCTV recordings), and others.
* Imposing the obligation for the drivers to have CCTVs turned on constantly might create reclass risks, but I’ll let [~accountid:610a3ee66051c5006aeeeea1] and [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] comment on this.
* On top of this, *we might have to implement product solutions*, allowing passengers to not take trips where CCTV is present with no charge.
* In addition, this will require a *local law analysis with external counsel,* as CCTV mandated by Bolt could be prohibited under local law (similar as to audio trip recording).



(?) _We want to work with a third party that records all videos (so the videos are not on the possession of neither the driver nor the rider) and if there is a safety issue, the driver or the rider can unilaterally allow Bolt to access that specific video recording and we can ask the partner to send the video to us._

💡 This could also imply that we’re in the possession of the recordings, instead of the drivers. This essentially means that the drivers have no control over the recordings, and therefore, in case of a claim, or a regulatory investigation, this argument can be used against us. Bottom line is that the fact that the driver doesn’t have the control over where this data is stored, and that ultimately Bolt is calling the shots (we can ask the partner to send the videos to us) means that we are responsible for CCTVs and not the drivers.



I am happy to jump on a call, however, I’d like to point out that the described initiative is *high risk* from a privacy POV, and at the moment we would not be able to launch this initiative without exposing us to risks as described above.



So far, it was my understanding that such projects, where Bolt will have access to recordings, or will impose the requirement to have CCTVs, or in any way control the use of CCTVs, will be done centrally. Adding [~accountid:5b7beb46b8624857f09efff9] for visibility on this - FYI.

Hello Greta! 

We had changes to this article a while ago because of cases where drives report to us: 

* If the driver reported taking the wrong rider, we needed to create a ticket to the rider. However, we are never sure if they will even except (lost money) or we are breaking our own BH guidelines for untagged outgoing cases. 
* No refund is to rider is faster, but leads to no action and potential for rider coming back anyway later wanting the refund and then we have to go back to driver. (wasted time).



To answer your first point, we can amend KB to be more clear like this: 

* If not already provided, ask the driver if they eventually still completed the ride with the correct rider:
** {color:#36b37e}*Trip happened with the correct rider:*{color}{color:#36b37e} If rider was overcharged, follow {color}{color:#36b37e}*🚗 Rider: I was charged more than expected.* {color}{color:#36b37e}If not, no further action necessary.{color}
** *Trip happened with the wrong rider:* Do not manually compensate the commission fee.
* Inform the driver about the compensation if provided.
* If the trip was not completed with the correct rider, send and outgoing message to the rider and refund the full price of the ride to the rider’s original payment method with _Driver_ as the actor at fault.
* Continue to Step 2.

h2. 

However, for point 2, I was informed by Legal previously that if the driver takes the wrong rider and never manages to complete trip with the right rider, we are not obligated to refund commission to the driver. Creating as ticket to the rider would lead to an untagged outgoing ticket and the rider potentially not accepting the refund.

Hey!

Oh my, this complicates things a bit. 

If they had no officially registered form of mutual co-existence, they are essentially left without a protection. 

Shortly:

* You are married: legal protection and you can ask for documents related to your spouse :green_circle: 
* You have a inheritance certificate/agreement: you can ask for documents related to your spouse :green_circle: 
* You had a registered union with your spouse: you can ask for documents related to your spouse :green_circle: 
* You are the child of the person, but your parents were not married: you can ask for documents related to the person :green_circle:
* You are the factual partner of the person, but you did not register the union: you don’t have the right to request such documents 🔴  

But! Should they have a power of attorney that was issued before the person passed, maybe we could work something out.

I completely understand the issue you raised, however, I’m afraid it won’t be possible for agents to determine if the pickup location was unreachable. Also, if the agent is not familiar with that particular place or the city, it will be hard for them to understand if the driver could have reached the exact pickup location or not.

Dear Chinyere,

As promised, I am getting back to you regarding your question about setting live of the two safety features - Driver Selfie Verification and Driving License Verification. Please find the analysis of the respective countries below:

# *Angola*

In Angola, biometric data processed for Selfie and Driving License Verification is considered "ordinary" personal data, not "sensitive."  While explicit consent is a standard legal basis for processing such data, Angolan law (specifically Article 12(2)(e)) also permits processing based on "legitimate interest."  This exception applies as long as the data subject's rights, freedoms, and guarantees are not overridden by the legitimate interest. Thus, in my view, *Bolt can rely on "legitimate interest"* as the legal basis for processing this biometric data, thereby avoiding the need to obtain driver consent.The risks associated with non-compliance are severe. It is estimated that they range from 195.000 USD to 390.000 USD.

*Example* from the DLA Piper Angola website: “_It is in our legitimate interest or a third party's legitimate interest to use your personal information in such a way to ensure that we provide the very best client service we can to you or others and comply with our professional and ethical duties as lawyers, consistent with applicable law_.”



*2. Zimbabwe*

Under Zimbabwean law, biometric data is classified as "sensitive personal data," unlike in Angola. This classification entails a higher level of protection. Therefore, before processing biometric data in Zimbabwe, Bolt must:

I. Provide prior notification to the Data Protection Authority; and
II. Obtain explicit written consent from each individual whose biometric data will be processed.

Based on current information, no applicable exception to these requirements exists for Bolt's intended use of biometric data.  As a result, implementing these features in Zimbabwe *will incur higher operational costs* and require more resources to ensure compliance with the law.

Fines for non-compliance entail both financial fines and imprisonment. Although the former are not clearly specified, the latter can end up with 7 years imprisonment.

Hi team, from an operational perspective, there are certain accounts we do not want to be deleted, as it will encourage even more fraud. Specifically:

* BQS long suspension: these accounts are already temporarily blocked for 1 year. The block will automatically lift at the ned of this timeframe
* Selfie ID verification failure, or any fraud events.
* Acceptance rate blocks. We currently do not have access to override these blocks.
* HP/Safety cases
* Accounts which owe commission
* T&Cs non compliance

The reason we cannot allow these accounts to be deleted is because then drivers will just be able to sign up again. Due to lead acceptance automation, there is a high chance these drivers would be back on the road, having been clearly identified as bad drivers.

There is also the case of drivers who request account deletion due to ignorance of our procedures. For example if drivers want to switch category from car to motorbike, or change city, they will often request to delete their account. 

Correct procedure would be to request the change through CS. We should look to add procedures to the KB article for these cases, so agents can guide the drivers to correctly upload documents etc.
These cases include:

* city change
* category change (car to moto/moto to car)
* audited auto acceptance leads which have incorrect/fake documents
* historic leads hidden for inactivity

Currently, the KB says:

* If not already mentioned, clarify if the driver wants to delete their account or just wants to drive in another city or company. If so, please follow [🚗 Driver: I want to start operating in another city|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360017522420]
* If they clarified that they want to delete their account, proceed with Step 2.

More emphasis needs to be made on understanding why the driver wants to delete their account, and then guide them to the correct way of achieving what they really want.

{quote}Dear Chinyere,

As promised, I am getting back to you regarding your question about setting live of the two safety features - Driver Selfie Verification and Driving License Verification. Please find the analysis of the respective countries below:{quote}

# *Angola*

{quote}In Angola, biometric data processed for Selfie and Driving License Verification is considered "ordinary" personal data, not "sensitive." While explicit consent is a standard legal basis for processing such data, Angolan law (specifically Article 12(2)(e)) also permits processing based on "legitimate interest."  This exception applies as long as the data subject's rights, freedoms, and guarantees are not overridden by the legitimate interest. Thus, in my view, *Bolt can rely on "legitimate interest"* as the legal basis for processing this biometric data, thereby avoiding the need to obtain driver consent.

*Example* from the DLA Piper Angola website: “_It is in our legitimate interest or a third party's legitimate interest to use your personal information in such a way to ensure that we provide the very best client service we can to you or others and comply with our professional and ethical duties as lawyers, consistent with applicable law_.”

*2. Zimbabwe*

Under Zimbabwean law, biometric data is classified as "sensitive personal data," unlike in Angola. This classification entails a higher level of protection. Therefore, before processing biometric data in Zimbabwe, Bolt must:

I. Provide prior notification to the Data Protection Authority (which we already obtain through a consent screen in the Selfie-Verification feature; and
II. Obtain explicit written consent from each individual whose biometric data will be processed.

h1. Proposed Solution

Given that the builder-agent already transmits all deployment data to Builder *and* that the HPA configuration is consistent across both clusters, we can establish the following approach:

When the number of pods for a service varies by more than 10% (to be determined) between different clusters, Builder can take the initiative to fine-tune the HPA target value. Specifically, it can lower this target by 2 points (or 2%, to be determined) in the Kubernetes cluster with fewer pods.

As a result, the HPA will be triggered more frequently in that cluster, leading to a more balanced distribution of pods across the clusters.

Following up with another comment, since I just saw that Teodor has also reached out to me in Slack 🙂 

I understand that the LL is opposed to purchasing all risks property policy, and is requiring us to buy that on behalf of the LL. For full visibility, this is what I have responded to Teodor in Slack as well: 

{quote}With regard to WHs, the relevant insurance coverage are the following:

* All risks property policy - covering any damage to the warehouse that is caused by natural disasters (such as fire, flooding, tsunami, earthquake etc), theft, burglary, or vandalism. This type of policy has to be purchased by the owner of the property; we as Bolt cannot buy such cover because we don’t have any “insurable interest” in the said property. Furthermore, sometimes real estate is encumbered by servitudes / mortgages / etc. which all affect the insurance coverage as well. As we do not own this property, then we do not have visibility on such matters, and therefore, are also not able to diligently follow our obligation of disclosure to the insurer. Overall - one person cannot insure another person’s property - the same way I cannot purchase a home insurance policy for your home.
* Operational liability policy - liability policy covers any damages that we might cause with our operations to the warehouse - e.g. charging station / batteries catch fire; a van backs into a wall; or our employees do not display due diligence, leaving the warehouse unlocked or unsurveillanced resulting in theft/burglary/vandalism - i.e. covering any damage that is a consequence to our operations. This policy can and *should* be bought by us. (I’ve also provided the details on this in my previous comment 🙂 )

However, if we are not able to achieve an agreement with the LL about the property insurance, and the LL does not want to bare the costs of the insurance policy, then perhaps we can agree that the landlord will incorporate the cost of the insurance policy into the rent fee.{quote}

Hey Thomas, to clarify:

* DOB/Nationality - *absolutely necessary*, as the local law can be changed at any time (as it has in the past) around these particular characteristics - driver age and nationality/citizenship (eg. EU, no EU, third countries etc). Legislative changes can take place at any time due to the current political climate, and several draft bills are currently being consulted with local stakeholders. We have to be ready to comply with any new regulations and these 2 data points are essential for this.
* Gender - as a company, Bolt offers "women4women" or "womendriver" category, where we promise users they will be picked up by a female driver. That is not possible to do if we don't gather and process this data. This is a global issue and it should be included in the T&Cs or the Privacy Notice on a Global level.

We would like to proceed with the changes to our local registration flows, as soon as possible and we are aligned on this with central ops. stakeholders. What is the potential timeline on your side to update T&Cs / Privacy Policy? If this is substantial (i.e. months, not days or weeks) we would like to understand the risks if we were to proceed with these changes before the documentation is updated.

{color:#bf2600}*Decision whether or not to compensate*{color}

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Damage compensation(s) claimed:*

# compensation for emotional distress
# cost of consulting lawyers
# costs related to transportation / time spent at the police station
# apology for providing inaccurate personal data to the police
{panel}

*82 GDPR* – Any person who suffered material non-material damage as a result of the infringement of GDPR has right to receive a compensation.

Unlawful processing of personal data → transmission of inaccurate personal data to the law enforcement authority → emotional distress + financial loss

Material damage - legal costs, costs related to visiting a police station

Non-material damage – emotional distress

* {color:#006644}Case C-300/21 Osterreichische Post{color} – Article 82 GDPR does not enable compensation to be ordered on the basis of an infringement of GDPR without first establishing damage that has been caused by that infringement. *Mere infringement of GDPR is not sufficient to confer right to compensation*.
* {color:#006644}Case C-182/22 and 189/22 Scalable Capital, Case 590/22 PS, Case C-300/21 Osterreichishce Post{color} – *person seeking compensation for non-material damage* on the basis of infringement of GDPR *is required to establish* not only the infringement but also *that the infringement has actually caused them such damage*.
* GDPR does not define rules on the assessment of damages → NPA (in this case Latvian law would apply on finding the conditions and reward amount)
* {color:#006644}Case C-507/23 Patērētāju tiesību aizsardzības centrs{color} – national court was asking whether an apology can constitute a sufficient remedy under Article 82 GDPR. CJEU held that in accordance with NPA, 82 GDPR does not preclude an apology to be a suitable compensation for non-material damage. (NB: This was a Latvian case where claimant was asking for compensation of non-material damage of reputation. The first instance NC awarded the claimant EUR 100). 



*Emotional distress x 82 GDPR*

* Again, “injured” person must actually prove emotional distress
* The bar for emotional distress seems quite high: [https://www.loyensloeff.com/insights/news--events/news/legal-framework-on-non-material-damages-under-the-gdpr-a-status-quo/|https://www.loyensloeff.com/insights/news--events/news/legal-framework-on-non-material-damages-under-the-gdpr-a-status-quo/|smart-link] 
* {color:#006644}Case C-667/21 Medizinishcer Dienst{color} – CJEU stressed that the right to compensation under Article 82 of the GDPR serves a compensatory, and not a punitive, function. Damages awarded under this provision should therefore fully cover the actual harm suffered from the GDPR violation, without extending to punitive or dissuasive amounts.

*Other*

* {color:#006644}Case C-741/21 GP v Juris GmbH{color}: merely showing that an employee (or person acting under the authority of the controller) failed to follow instructions, leading to the damage, is not sufficient for the controller to be exempted from liability.

Response from AMT on *16/01/2025*

[^Oficio nº 00267_16JAN_PLMJ_Bolt (1) (626733cc-f900-4ce8-8f52-c35b336563bf).pdf]

*Summary and next steps by PLMJ:*

We had a closer look at the AMT decision regarding the administrative complaint submitted by Bolt on 28 August 2024. In the decision, the AMT has reinforced its Opinion No. 37/AMT/2024, which determined that the provision of taxi transport services via an electronic platform under the contractual taxi fare model (Tariff C) is not legally compliant.

AMT has sent the official deliberation to our offices. Please advise on where we should resend the document.

Also, please find below our notes on the decision for your convenience and potential next steps.

*i.            Legal Grounds for the Decision*

* +Regulatory & Competitive Concerns:+ While the model aligns with contractual tariff requirements, its +pricing structure and geographical flexibility+ create potential +market distortions+, allowing taxi operators on the platform to circumvent standard taxi fare regulations and restrictions applicable to non-platform taxis.  Additionally, the AMT maintains that Tariff C should not be used as a generalised alternative to metered fares.
* +Non-Compliance with the Legal Framework+: The AMT affirms the model +conflicts with Article 22(3) of Decree-Law No. 101/2023 and Article 2(4) of Law No. 45/2018+, as it enables services that resemble TVDE operations without adhering to the corresponding regulatory framework. 
* +Lack of Effective Oversight+: The AMT affirms Bolt has not provided sufficient mechanisms to +supervise compliance+ with municipal taxi quotas, nor has it demonstrated an +effective allocation system+ to prevent taxis from operating outside their licensed geographic areas.
* +Pending Regulatory Developments+*:* The +new AMT Tariff Regulation+ will explicitly govern fixed-price digital taxi bookings, and the AMT considers that Bolt should await its publication before implementing this pricing model.

*ii.           Potential Legal Grounds for the Judicial Appeal*

Following our preliminary analysis of the AMT’s decision, we have identified critical aspects and/or inconsistencies that may serve as grounds for a judicial appeal, including:

* +Misalignment with the AMT’s Own Regulatory Framework:+ The AMT contends that the contractual taxi fare model infringes regulatory and competitive principles, citing issues with geographic contingencies and alleged market distortions. However, the AMT has not provided sufficient evidence to substantiate claims of abuse or regulatory non-compliance under Tariff C.

Additionally, Bolt has demonstrated its commitment to ensuring compliance with geographic contingencies, including the development of in-app solutions to address potential gaps. Providing the AMT with examples of these in-app measures could effectively counter their assertions.

* +Inconsistencies with the Draft Tariff Regulation+: The Draft Tariff Regulation, specifically Article 12, explicitly permits three pricing models, including Tariff C. This suggests that the AMT’s current enforcement action against Tariff C is at odds with its own forthcoming regulatory framework.
* +Economic and Financial Recovery Principles+: The AMT’s concerns regarding Tariff C are that it allegedly hinders the economic and financial recovery principles outlined in Article 20, no. 1, of Decree-Law No. 101/2023. Bolt’s argument shall focus on the fact that the Tariff C fare model provides a balance between operational cost recovery and passenger affordability, which was not initially used in the administrative complaint.
* +Role of Bolt in Pricing Determination+: Contrary to the AMT’s assertions, Bolt does not unilaterally determine the final price for trips under the Tariff C model. It should be reinforced (as stated in the administrative complaint) that for metered fares, Bolt only provides an estimated price range as a reference, which is non-binding, and that the final price is determined by the taximeter.

Strategically, a potential advantage of filing a lawsuit would be stress Bolt’s position of principle in courts and, separately, engage with AMT again to attempt a balance of positions.

*iii.          Judicial Appeal Deadline*

 Should Bolt wish to challenge this decision in court, the deadline to file an appeal is *16 April 2025* (3 months deadline, as per article 58, no. 1 paragraph a) of the PT Administrative Procedural Code).

 Please let us know if you require further clarification or support regarding the next steps.

In the new T&Cs we will be able to referring to a certain level of behaviour/ car quality rather than a rating, which does not mean that we can’t use a rating.

* The only market where the rating system can’t be used bcs of reclass is Switzerland.
* The issue we have to suspend only bcs of a low average rating is that the rating itself does not say anything about what has went wrong. Therefore the suspension reason can not rely on a low average rating if we can’t provide any further information (was it a certain level of behaviour, if yes which one). The reason for suspension is e.g. discomfort and the evidence we have is average low rider rating or a low rider rating such as a safety incident etc.
So not having the average driver rating is not a blocker, *the blocker is being intransparent with the blocking reason itself*. 
* *All Driver need to be informed about the min. average rating* but moreover all drivers need to be *informed about what has impact on the average rating* and why we are doing this. These communications are *subject to legal review*. Ideally the rating would/ should start from scratch (when we pretend it’s now implemented).
* An immediate suspension can only happen *based on serious and evident safety cases or investigation purposes*. 3 times a smelly car? Not really a reason for an immediate termination.
* As I have already highlighted the defence narrative which we should stick to is: “_You have done XYZ which is in breach of our platform terms and the evidence for this is low average rating_” NOT “_Hey, thanks. We block you bcs of your low average rating!_”
